text: Problem management exists to reduce the likelihood and impact of incidents, by identifying actual and potential causes and managing workarounds and known errors — the ITIL 4 purpose statement in full. A problem is a cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents. Where incident management chases speed above everything, problem management chases depth. It's allowed to take longer, because its payoff isn't one user unblocked right now — it's an entire failure mode stopping, or hurting far less next time.

Problems don't announce themselves the way incidents do, so problem identification is active work: analyzing trends across many incidents — the same error on five different servers this month — reviewing a major incident afterward, or a vendor flagging a known defect. A single incident rarely proves a problem exists on its own. It's usually a repeating pattern, or one severe occurrence, that actually triggers the investigation.

Once identified, problem control analyzes and prioritizes it. This is root-cause-analysis territory — digging into logs, configurations, and change history to understand why the failure keeps happening, not just that it does. Not every identified problem gets equal attention. Problem control assigns priority based on impact and likelihood, aimed at future incidents this cause could still produce.

Once root cause is understood but a permanent fix isn't in place yet — it needs a vendor patch, a budget approval, or a scheduled change — the problem becomes a known error: analyzed, but not yet permanently resolved. Error control manages known errors through to resolution, and tracks whatever workaround is in use, so future incidents from the same cause resolve faster even before the real fix lands.

The defining boundary: problem management is never judged by how fast one incident gets fixed — that's incident management's job, happening in parallel with a workaround while investigation continues. Problem management is judged by whether the failure keeps coming back. A workaround applied ten times a month means the real cause is still there, still costing the business — until something actually changes the configuration or code at fault. That's where change enablement enters next.
